title: Probability and Conditional Probability, Part 3: Traps and the Fast Way

beats.say: In this video, we look at five mistakes students make with probability, and then the fast way: name the denominator first, and use complements.

card.text: Five traps, then the fast way

beats.say: Each trap is shown as a wrong line first, then the right line, with the reason it's so tempting.
Trap one. For under thirty, given that the customer shops online, students divide by the grand total of one hundred seventy.
The words given that shrink the group to the online customers. So the denominator is seventy-five.
Trap two. The probability of online given under thirty is different from the probability of under thirty given online. They share the same numerator, but not the same denominator.
Given under thirty, the group is the Under thirty row, with a total of eighty. So the probability of online is forty-eight over eighty.

scenes.title: Trap 3: forgetting to reduce the total

beats.say: Trap three. Without replacement, once a tile has been drawn, there are fewer tiles left. Students keep the same total for the second draw.
After one tile is removed, eleven tiles remain. So the second fraction is four over eleven, not four over twelve.
Trap four. For this and then that, with independent events, you multiply the probabilities. Students add them instead.
The chance that both happen is smaller than either chance alone. One half times one sixth is one twelfth.
Trap five. Two spins each land on an even number with probability one third. For at least one even, students add the two probabilities, and double count the case where both spins are even.
Use the complement. The chance of no even number on either spin is two thirds times two thirds. Subtracting from one gives five ninths.
Probability on the SAT is counting, so Desmos is only a calculator here. The fast way is to name the denominator before looking for the numerator.
Underline the group after the words given, of the, or selected from, and find that total first. Then count how many of that group fit the question.
For percent-based questions, imagine a convenient total, such as one thousand people, and convert each percent to a count. Then read the answer as a fraction of counts.

Desmos helps with messy arithmetic. Seventy percent of items come from machine A, with a four percent defect rate, and thirty percent from machine B, with a ten percent rate. Given a defective item, what's the probability it came from A?
Open a fresh graph. We'll type the whole fraction in one line, so nothing is rounded along the way.
Type the numerator in parentheses, zero point seven times zero point zero four, then a slash, and the denominator in parentheses, the same product plus zero point three times zero point one.
Desmos shows about zero point four eight three. So the probability that a defective item came from machine A is about forty-eight percent.
Now a practice problem. Two spins each land on an even number with probability one third. What's the probability of at least one even number? Pause the video, try it, and then watch the solution.
The probability of no even number on one spin is two thirds. Both spins are independent, so the probability of no even on both spins is two thirds times two thirds.
Two thirds times two thirds is four ninths. So the probability of no even number on either spin is four ninths.
One is nine ninths, and nine ninths minus four ninths is five ninths. So the probability of at least one even number is five ninths.
Check by counting the cases directly. Even then not even is one third times two thirds, not even then even is two thirds times one third, and even then even is one third times one third.
To recap. Name the denominator first, and don't swap the condition in a conditional probability.
beats.item: Name the denominator; keep the condition

beats.say: Reduce the total without replacement, multiply for this and then that, and use the complement for at least one.
Use Desmos as a calculator for messy arithmetic. In the next topic, we study inference and margin of error.
